title: TA9-11520
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision in the claim of, XXXXXXXXXXX, who claims to be a citizen of China and who is claiming refugee protection pursuant to Section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 Edited for syntax and grammar, as well as, I will add references to applicable case law and any other documentary evidence as may be necessary.

The claimant alleges that in 2009, he became friends with two Taiwanese preachers who introduced him to Christianity. In XXXX 2009, the claimant allowed his friends to use his grandfather's vacant home as a site where they could preach the gospel and hold underground church services. The claimant alleges that he assisted the preachers by interpreting on their behalf and that in the course of doing so he became a Christian. In XXXX 2009, the head of the village committee, asked the preachers to register the church, however they refused. On XXXX, 2009, the church was raided by members of the Public Security Bureau. All 18 congregants were arrested along with the two preachers. In addition all of the bibles were seized. Upon hearing this, the claimant went into hiding. He subsequently learned that the Public Security Bureau went to his home looking for him. Fearing he would be arrested the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China for Canada where he filed a refugee protection claim.

I find on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection; the reasons are as follows. The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the claimant's oral testimony and documentary evidence in regard to his identity as a Christian. In this regard, I find that the claimant was not a credible witness. The reasons for the decision are hereby noted.

The claimant alleges that 18 of his fellow church members were arrested and that each was held for a period of six months and fined 5,000 Yuan. The claimant also alleges that the two pastors were subsequently deported. The claimant's testimony in this regard runs counter to the country condition documents which I will discuss later in these reasons with the analysis of the situation of Christians in Fujian province. In this regard I draw a negative inference.

The claimant alleges that the PSB have attended his home on nine occasions with the intent of arresting him and that they have continued to pursue him as late as XXXX of 2011. The claimant tendered a document entitled Notice of Summoning2 that he alleged was left with his family after the raid on XXXX, 2009. I have noted a number of concerns with the summons which causes me to question its genuineness.

The documentary evidence regarding the issuance of a summons notes that a summons would almost always be issued to the individual rather than a household or a family member. However, it also noted that it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave the summons with family members instructing them to pass it along to the persons named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgement of receipt. Although this is not actually the proper procedure it happens all the time, especially in cases when a person in the summons is not easily locatable.3

The documentary evidence also notes the format and appearances of summons; it states that the notice is prepared in triplicate. The original is kept at the police station, the duplicate copy is signed, dated and returned by the suspect and one copy is left with the suspect. The summons tendered by the claimant includes a section that is an acknowledgement that the summons was received; however this section has been left blank with no signature or acknowledgement of receipt by anybody. This is not consistent with the documentary evidence as noted above.

A summons is either issued to the person named in the summons or to a family or household member and the person who receives the summons is expected to sign in that regard. I also note that the summons that was tendered did not identify the claimant's address on the face of the document, which is also not consistent with the sample in the document in the national documentation package.

The claimant's counsel has submitted that there may be substantial differences in the type of information on summons' issued by PSB offices. However, I prefer the evidence of the China country documentation in regard to the issuance of summonses, as this information is provided by unbiased independent sources with no interest in the outcome of any particular refugee claim.

Further, it is reasonable to expect that a Public Security Bureau document would include the address of the person named on the summons since this information would be required by the serving officer to correctly identify the location of the individual's known address and to affect service of the document.

In addition, upon further review of the document I note that there is no serial number on the face of the summons which also does not correspond with the sample contained in the National Documentation Package. I further note that the summons tendered by the claimant bears what appears to be an official seal of the Public Security Bureau. It is my belief that the purpose of the seal is to seal the document in order to demonstrate the document has not been altered or tampered with. However, the seal on this summons has handwriting which has been written over the seal thereby undermining the intended purpose of the seal. On the basis of the inconsistencies in the summons provided by the claimant I can give little weight to this document.

The claimant alleges that the claimant used the services of a smuggler to leave China and travel to Canada. The claimant was asked if he knew the name in the passport that was used by him to leave China and travel to Canada. The claimant stated that the claimant only glanced at the passport and saw that his picture was in it but saw no other information. The claimant did not know the colour of the passport or which country issued the passport. The claimant was asked what instructions were provided to him by the smuggler in the event he was questioned by airport or security officials while in transit. The claimant testified that the smuggler told him not to worry because she had persons in place. However, in addition to not knowing the name he was travelling under or which country he was purporting to be a citizen of, the claimant also did not know what type of passport the smuggler was using or what name the smuggler was using to travel; despite the fact that the smuggler and the claimant were travelling together. While I do recognize the need for the board to be sensitive to the vulnerabilities of claimants travelling under false documents I do not find that it excuses the claimant for his testimonial failings concerning the lack of knowledge of the identity he was travelling under.

The fact that the claimant claimed to be following instructions of the smuggler does not explain why he could not relate anything of significance about the identities he and the smuggler were travelling under. I find it neither plausible nor credible that the claimant would not be aware of this basic information in the face of the obvious likelihood that he would be questioned about it in transit.

The claimant testified that during the raid of the underground house church all of the bibles were seized by the Public Security Bureau. Documentary evidence states that the Public Security Bureau will issue a receipt for items that are seized in the course of an investigation.4 The claimant was questioned with respect to the issuance of receipts by the PSB and the claimant's testimony was that there were no receipts. Given that the Public Security Bureau has allegedly issued a summons to the claimant it would appear that in the claimant's case they are not averse to following the rule of law.

As such it is reasonable to expect that a receipt would have been issued for the seizure or confiscation of bibles at the time of the raid if it had occurred. I draw a negative inference from the lack of receipt issued for the confiscation of bibles. Based on the foregoing findings and negative inferences I find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant is not being pursued by the Public Security Bureau as he has alleged.

With respect to the claimant's identity as a Christian, the claimant alleges that he became involved in Christianity in XXXX 2009 but did not believe in Christianity until one month after meeting the preachers from Taiwan. The claimant alleges that the church was raided approximately a month after he became a Christian.

The claimant was asked a number of questions concerning his religious knowledge. While the claimant was able to answer most questions it was clear that he did not have a clear understanding of the concept of absolution of sin as it relates to the crucifixion and death of Jesus. The claimant testified that the death of Jesus absolved mankind of both original sin and "principal" sin. Christians believe that the absolution of original sin only comes through baptism. It is reasonable to expect that the claimant would know this distinction. In this regard I draw a negative inference.

While the claimant was able to demonstrate some knowledge of Christianity that knowledge does not necessarily mean that the claimant is a genuine practicing Christian. The claimant produced a baptismal certificate and two letters from Reverend XX5 The letters indicate that the claimant has been attending church in Canada since XXXX of 2009. These documents can only attest to the claimant's participation in church activities, they do not attest to his motivation. In this regard recent case law indicates that a pastor's assessment on the genuineness of a person's faith can not be substituted for the assessment the panel is required to make.6 Given the foregoing I give little weight to the letter from Reverend XX in assessing the genuineness of the claimant's Christian faith.

While it is difficult to make a judgment regarding the genuineness of a person's religious practice, it is necessary in this case. In doing so I have considered the totality of the evidence available, having previously found that the claimant's testimony concerning the claimant's alleged house church in China untrustworthy, I further find on a balance of probabilities that the claimant was not a Christian in China. I further find that the claimant's allegation that he was a practicing Christian in China is not credible and was only made for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent claim.

Having found that you were not a Christian in China I must consider whether you are a genuine practicing Christian in this country. There is a requirement for good faith in making a refugee claim. In this regard, R.P.G. Haines, the Chairman of a refugee status appeal panel and A.G. Wang Heed, a member of the United Nations High Commission for Refugees stated in part: If there is no good faith requirement in the sur place situation, it places in the hands of the appellant for refugee status the means of unilaterally determining the grant to him or her of refugee status.7

In this regard, the panel cites the following from James Hathaway's The Law of Refugee Status with regard to "sur place" claims: An individual who as a stratagem deliberately manipulates circumstances to create a real chance of persecution, which did not exist, cannot be said to belong to this category.8 The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, and in the context of all of the findings and negative inferences drawn above, that this claim has not been made in good faith.

Having found that the claimant are not a genuine practicing Christian in China and having found that this claim has not been made in good faith I find, on a balance of probabilities, and, in the context of the findings I have previously noted, that the claimant joined a Christian church in Canada only for the purpose of supporting a fraudulent refugee claim. In the context as noted and on the basis of the totality of the evidence disclosed and in the context of the claimant's Christian knowledge I find that the claimant is not a genuine practicing Christian nor would he be perceived to be in China. Situation of Christians in Fujian Province

Notwithstanding the foregoing determination, in the alternative, the panel has considered whether there is a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted if he returns to China and chooses to practice Christianity in an unregistered church. The panel is guided by the Country Condition Documents in evidence.9 The claimant is from Fujian province. The panel notes the documentary evidence suggests by virtue of the absence of evidence of incidents of persecution that Fujian and Guangdong have the most liberal policy on religion in China. The Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council recently stated in XXXX, 2010 correspondence that the Chinese authorities have demonstrated a high degree of tolerance to Christian activities in general and particularly towards non-registered groups.10

The panel also notes that though there were arrests of Christians documented in 2005, 2006, 2007 and 2008, 2009 and 2010 none of these arrests were noted as being in Fujian province. In 2005, there were reports of house church crackdowns in the provinces of Shanxi, Henan, Hubei, Jiangxi, and Jilin and in May 2005, Chinese officials coordinated raids on 100 house churches in Jilin province [northeast China], arresting approximately 600 Christians.11 During the year, there were also reports of similar incidents in Hebei, Xinjiang, Beijing and Shanghai.12 The U.S. 2009 International Religious Freedom Report13 specifically reviews arrests of Christians in China in 2007 and 2008 and 2009 and notes arrests of Christians in Beijing, the XUAR, Jilin province, Hebei province, Guangxi province, Gansu province and Shaanxi province. No mention is made of arrests of Christians in Fujian province in 2007 and 2008. A review of the most recent articles14 in the exhibits covering 2008 and 2009 has revealed that there have been arrests of Christians in Beijing, Jilin province, Xinjiang province, Guizhou province, Hubei province, Hebei province, Inner Mongolia, the XUAR, Henan province, Sichuan province, Shandong province, Zhejiang province, Anhui province, Jiangsu province, Yunnan province and Gansu province. However, there have been no such arrests in Fujian province. Documentary evidence submitted does not provide any recent evidence of arrests of Christians in Fujian province.

The Annual Report of Persecution by the Government on Christian Churches within Mainland China15 very specifically notes the arrests and incidents of persecution of Christians in China from January 2009 to December 2009, but no arrests occurred in Fujian province where the claimant is from. This report states that during 2009, the number of Christians persecuted in all of China was 2,935 and that the number of Christians arrested and detained was 389 representing a decrease of 49% from the previous year. Of the 389 persons arrested, 211 were church leaders, which accounts for 54.2 % of all people arrested and 9.3% of all people persecuted. The report also states that 23 people were sentenced in 2009 representing a drop of 34.3 5 from the year previous. There is no information in the report which identifies the percentage of church leaders sentenced. The panel has reviewed all the documentary evidence submitted and finds no evidence of recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province.

The China Aid Association's (CAA) 2010 annual report states that ten persons were persecuted in Fujian province in 2010. A review of the CAA report by the panel reveled that one incident was reported at a Lianjiang County church. The reports states that three venues used for the church gatherings were closed and that one church staffer was detained. Although the report states that ten persons were persecuted, there is no information how these persons were persecuted or why the churches were sealed. In fact, it is not clear from the report if the church is a registered or an unregistered church. As such, the panel can give the report little weight in assessing the over risk of persecution of Christians in Fujian. What is clear, however, there is no information in the report that persons were arrested or sentenced for underground church activities.

The panel has considered all of the documents submitted about the situation for Christians in China, specifically the articles and reports documenting arrests and persecution. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that if there were recent arrests of Christians in Fujian province, there would be some documentation of these arrests.

The principle asserted in Maldonado16 is that when a refugee claimant swears to the truth of certain allegations, a presumption is created that those allegations are true unless there are reasons to doubt their truthfulness. However, the presumption that a claimant's own testimony is true is always rebuttable and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.17

The claimant testified that all 18 members were arrested and detained for six months and fined and the two leaders of the church were deported. There are a number of observers, such as the China Aid Association, the US department of State, the Holy Spirit Study Centre, AsiaNews.it (which provides information on ecclesiastic communities in Asia), numerous news agencies, Cardinal Fung Foundation, Freedom House18 to name a few. These observers strive to inform the world that religious persecution takes place in China. In the case of underground Christian house churches, there is information detailing very specific examples of persecution from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian province. One would expect that and an egregious incident such as alleged by the claimant would be reported.

The panel is supported in this analysis by a recent Federal Court decision19 by Justice Crampton who found that it was reasonable for the panel to find that, if underground Christians faced a serious possibility of persecution in Fujian Province, it would have been documented. The decision goes on to find that the panel was not unreasonable to differentiate between the treatment of Catholics and underground Protestants in Fujian.

The panel concedes that China Aid Association (CAA) has stated in its report and letters that they have not documented all cases of persecution and religious repression occurring in every province in China, including Guangdong and Fujian. However, I note again that there has been no mention at all of recent arrests of lay Christians in Fujian province in any of the documentation regarding religious persecution in China and according to the latest U.S. Department of State International Freedom of Religion Report,20 the extent of religious freedom in China continues to vary widely within the country. That report notes that unregistered religious groups have continued to expand and that most Christian groups, the majority of which are not registered, no longer operate in strict secrecy21 and in fact carried out public activities including convening seminars, publishing materials, renting space for offices and events, and disseminating information on the Internet. Many unregistered religious groups also carried out social service work. Both registered and unregistered faith-based organizations ran clinics, homes for the elderly, orphanages and social centers.22 In some regions, government supervision of religious activity was minimal with registered and unregistered churches existing openly and receiving similar treatment by the authorities.23 In parts of the country, unregistered groups grew rapidly and authorities did not pressure them to register.24 The panel finds that the situation in Fujian province does not reflect what is happening in many other provinces where there have been arrests of ordinary Christians.

The British Home Office Report notes that there are fifty to seventy million Protestant Christians in China who practice without state sanction and that only twenty million practice their religion in state approved churches.25 That report also states that prayer meetings and Bible study groups held among friends and families need not register with authorities.26

As has been discussed, the supporting documentary evidence for the claimant's home province of Fujian indicates, the risk of persecution for practicing Christians is low. The panel recognizes that even if the evidence speaks of some harm that would qualify as serious, the panel must consider whether there is a serious possibility that the harm will actually come to pass. A statute, which outlaws the claimant's conduct or characteristic, may be in existence, and it may provide for unconscionably severe punishment for that conduct or characteristic, but this does not necessarily mean there is a serious possibility that the punishment will be inflicted on the claimant. The Supreme Court has emphasized that, in a determination as to whether the claimant's fear is objectively well founded, the relevant factors include the laws in the claimant's homeland, together with the manner in which they are applied. In this connection, the Court cited paragraph 43 of the UNHCR Handbook. 27

This leads the panel to determine, that the claimant is free to choose to worship in the Christian congregation of her choosing. The panel has chosen to rely on the documentary evidence because it originates from a variety of reputable independent sources, which would reasonably be expected to be knowledgeable with respect to the situation of Christians in Fujian. The documentary evidence is seen as reliable, probative, detailed information, so as to provide the panel with a thorough understanding of the situation of the Christian Church in Fujian province.

The panel has considered the documentary evidence and the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to practice his religion in any church in Fujian province if he were to return to his home in Fujian province in China and that there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for doing so.

The panel is supported in this decision by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell.28 While this decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong Province, the profile of Fujian province is virtually identical in terms of country document evidence concerning policies and actions concerning membership in underground Christian churches. In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin29 concerning Fujian province in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province it would have been documented. In addition, Justice Lemieux in Jiang30 noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice and people generally practice their religion freely.

Further, in Yu,31 Justice Zinn noted that the only evidence provided to the Board regarding an alleged raid was the claimant's own testimony. It was further noted that although the claimant in that case had been found to be credible in regard to his Christian identity and membership in a house church, there was documentary evidence before the Board that brought his evidence of the raid into question and lead to an inference that no such raid occurred.

In the more recent Federal Court decision in the case of Yao,32 Justice O'Keefe notes that "this Court has held on several occasions that the Board's finding that Christian may practice freely in Fujian province is reasonable."

On the basis of the totality of the evidence and the cumulative findings and negative inferences noted above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim.
